name: Heavy cream / butter diet

card.summary: A very high-fat dairy take on low-carb eating; nobody has trialled it for looks, and butter raises LDL.
card.note: Very high saturated fat intake raises LDL cholesterol.

quick.overview:
This is a low-carbohydrate approach in which butter and heavy cream provide most calories. It is discussed as a simple high-fat option related to keto.

No studies have tested it specifically for fat loss or appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Butter and cream supply fat with almost no carbohydrate, which proponents say helps with fullness and with staying in ketosis. These claims have not been tested for this exact pattern.
quick.risks: Butter is high in saturated fat and raises LDL cholesterol relative to plant oils, according to cited reviews. Health bodies such as the NHS advise limiting it. Ketogenic diets can cause constipation, lipid changes and kidney stones.

lead: The heavy cream / butter diet is a high-fat dairy variant of low-carbohydrate eating, in which large amounts of butter and cream supply a major share of calories. People in appearance communities use it as a way to lose body fat and get leaner, to simplify meals while eating very low carbohydrate, and sometimes to stay in ketosis.[1][2][3]

Butter is made by churning cream and is about 81 percent butterfat, with almost no carbohydrate or protein and roughly 51 g of saturated fat per 100 g.[1] The pattern overlaps with ketogenic eating, a high-fat, low-carbohydrate approach whose established medical use is drug-resistant epilepsy.[2] Low-carbohydrate diets in general can produce more early weight loss than low-fat diets, an advantage that reviews describe as shrinking over time, and a 2022 Cochrane review found no benefit over balanced diets at two years.[3]

Wikipedia reports that replacing plant oils with butter raises LDL cholesterol, and controlled feeding trials have compared butter with other dairy fats on blood lipids.[1][4][5] No clinical studies of a diet centred on heavy cream and butter for appearance outcomes were located.

chain: Butter and cream supply fat with almost no carbohydrate
Very-low-carbohydrate eating is used as a route to a calorie deficit and fullness
Lower body fat and a leaner face and waist
angle.text: People use the pattern to reduce body fat by keeping carbohydrate very low and meals simple. The route to a leaner look depends on overall calories, which is how trial reviews of low-carbohydrate diets frame weight loss.

infobox: About 81% butterfat; about 51 g saturated fat per 100 g[1]

paras: Butter contains almost no carbohydrate or protein.[1] A diet built around butter and cream overlaps with ketogenic eating, a high-fat, low-carbohydrate pattern whose established medical use is in drug-resistant epilepsy.[2] Wikipedia notes that low-carbohydrate diets have no standard threshold; the American Academy of Family Physicians uses under 20 percent of calories from carbohydrate and the National Lipid Association uses under 10 percent for 'very low'.[3]

Low-carbohydrate diets can produce more weight loss than low-fat diets in the short to medium term, with the Endocrine Society (2017) putting the early advantage at about 100 kcal per day, which fades. A 2022 Cochrane review found no benefit over balanced diets at two years, and a 2017 review concluded that calorie restriction and adherence drive results more than diet type.[3]

A randomized crossover trial in 23 adults compared liquid meals containing 30 g of fat from heavy cream, olive oil, sunflower, flaxseed and fish oil. Energy expenditure and substrate oxidation did not differ between fat sources, and satiety responses were not changed by the degree of saturation.[6]

The UK NHS advises eating butter less often and in small amounts.[1] A 2016 meta-analysis cited on Wikipedia found small or non-significant associations between about 14 g per day of butter and mortality or cardiovascular disease.[1] Evidence on cancer is mixed, with a 2021 meta-analysis finding no significant increase and a 2025 US cohort study reporting higher risk compared with plant oils.[1]

In a 2004 crossover study of 14 young men, fasting LDL cholesterol was significantly higher after a butter diet than after a cheese diet.[4] A 2017 trial in 92 adults with abdominal obesity found LDL cholesterol higher after butter than cheese, and both higher than after monounsaturated, polyunsaturated or high-carbohydrate diets.[5]

Ketogenic diets in clinical settings are linked to constipation, raised blood lipids and kidney stones, and are started under medical supervision.[2] Wikipedia lists constipation, headache, halitosis, muscle cramps and weakness among reported low-carbohydrate side effects, and says very low-carbohydrate eating makes adequate fiber hard to get.[3]

No studies found on a heavy cream and butter diet for fat loss or appearance. Related trials examined dairy fats and blood lipids, and fat sources and postprandial energy expenditure, rather than appearance outcomes.[4][5][6]
